name: Carlos Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a small procurement team at a building materials company, four buyers who buy cement, timber, steel bar and the rest from suppliers. My day is checking prices, signing off orders over the buyers' limits, haggling with a couple of big suppliers by phone and sitting in the weekly stock meeting with the yard managers. I've had the job about ten months. The buyers under me are older than me and one of them, Henrik, clearly thinks he should've got it, and he's probably right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On Saturdays I coach the under-tens at the football club near my parents' place. My dad runs a little car repair garage there, he's done it for thirty years. I bought my own flat two years ago, small but it's mine. I use AI now and then to compare supplier quotes, once a colleague showed me it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Building is old-fashioned and slow, and the suppliers still want a phone call. I'd say that in the stock meeting and probably to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, because I'm still getting the hang of managing older guys like Henrik. A quiet few years to prove myself would suit me fine. My flat's mine and I've got a good pile saved, so money's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and get better at it. I'd use the quote-comparing tool a bit more, since it saves me an hour a day, and maybe show the buyers. I'd keep coaching on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most want from those quiet years at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Respect, mostly. I'd ask Henrik to show me how he handles the steel suppliers. A quiet year would give me time to earn the respect of a buyer like Henrik (the older colleague who wanted my job), instead of just having the title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still be at the club on Saturday and at Mum's for Sunday lunch. That's how I like it.

His **own flat** and savings mean money's fine.

Ask **Henrik** to teach him how to handle steel suppliers.

steps.text: Ask Henrik to teach him the steel supplier negotiations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the market, and the companies that use it well will win. I'm not one for blocking progress. But I'd also say a firm owes its loyal people a chance to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, buying is right there on the list. My buyers compare prices, place orders and chase deliveries, and software will do most of that. I think the team goes from four to two, and a junior manager who's still learning is not the safest seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the buying software now, once I'd seen the other buyers struggle with it. I'd put more into savings and pay a chunk off the flat, so I'm not carrying much debt. And I'd ask to spend more time on the yard and site side, where you're dealing with trucks and contractors face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sort of a knot that doesn't go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henrik, probably, which is strange given he doesn't like me. I feel sick for Henrik (the senior buyer on my team), who has twenty-two years in the job and no idea how the new software works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Henrik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help him learn it, whether he likes me or not. That's how my dad would do it.

steps.text: Learn the new buying software once others have tested it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock, and people should lean on their families and get back to real skills. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not just send cheques. That's what I'd say at the club and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone by 2028, procurement is all thinking work. Even the yard side changes fast once the AI plans everything. The one place I can see some years is my dad's garage, because fixing a car is hands-on and robots are about three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go and work with my dad at the garage and learn the trade properly from him. I'd put some savings into new diagnostic kit for electric cars, so the garage isn't stuck in the past. I'd keep the flat, it's paid down enough to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, though he'd hide it. My dad (who has run his garage for thirty years) always wanted me in the business, and it would take the end of office work to get me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is three years in the garage enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only three years, and then the robots come for car repair too. I know that. But three years with my dad, learning his trade, is worth something.

say: I'd tell people to lean on **family** and real skills.
I'd want government to back **apprenticeships**, not just send cheques.
think: Procurement is **gone by 2028**, as pure thinking work.
His dad's **garage** gives some years, with robots three years behind.
do: Join his **dad's garage** and learn the trade.
Buy **diagnostic kit** for electric cars with savings.
Keep the **flat**, which is paid down enough to manage.
S2.quote: My dad (who has run his garage for thirty years) always wanted me in the business, and it would take the end of office work to get me there.
fieldNote: The **family garage** is his fallback, and he uses the robot gap.

steps.text: Join his dad's garage and learn car repair from him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so people should get a skill they can use with their hands. I'd say it to the parents at the club. At work I'd say let's use the time well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have three or four years in procurement, then it ends. I'm open to the AI in the meantime, because it'd help me do the job while it lasts. The bigger question is what my dad's garage looks like when he wants to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the buying AI properly at work, so I'm good at the job while it lasts. I'd do an evening course in vehicle mechanics, electric cars especially, for two years. Then around year three I'd go into the garage with my dad and start taking it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the garage when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in charge before the robots come, and I'd buy whatever robots help. If robots arrive three years after the AI, I want to be the man who owns the garage, not the mechanic it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be at the end of the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32, single or not, I don't know. My mum would say married. I'd say: a business first, then we'll see.

fieldNote: He plans to **own** rather than work in the garage, buying robots himself.
Five years lets him **retrain** before joining the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people who work hard will find their place. I'd say families and firms should plan, not wait for the government. That's my view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty comfortable. Ten years is a long time in procurement, I'd likely be head of buying by then. And I'd have time to plan the garage properly with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the building materials firm and aim for a head of procurement job in five or six years. I'd keep saving and pay off the flat. Around year seven I'd start the mechanics course and plan the garage handover for when Dad turns 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you leaving it a bit late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Ten years is long enough that I'd be tempted to leave everything to the last minute, which is exactly what my dad would tell me not to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want outside work in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marriage, kids, the club. I'd want to be coaching my own son's team one day. That's what I want the ten years for.

I'd tell families and firms to **plan**, not wait for government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the garage would be a rush job instead of a plan, and my buyers would all be out at once. What would help is apprenticeships for grown adults, paid, so a 40-year-old buyer can learn a trade without starving. I don't need anyone to look after me, I need a way to learn a real trade at 30 without starting from nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about Henrik. He's 51 and I'd worry about him in every picture, even though he can't stand me. People like him built the company.

headlineQuote: I don't need anyone to look after me, I need a way to learn a real trade at 30 without starting from nothing.
portrait: Carlos is **27** and manages four buyers at a building materials company, with an older buyer resenting his promotion.
He owns a **small flat**, has strong savings, and coaches under-tens on Saturdays.
He uses AI **once it's proven**, and leans to free markets and apprenticeships.
His fallback in every fast picture is his dad's **car repair garage**.
He'd rather **own** the garage and its robots than be the mechanic replaced.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, turning the garage move into a rush **job**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults learning a trade later in life.
